overall_summary: The channel's performance is heavily driven by extreme space anomalies and exoplanet mysteries, particularly those featuring high-contrast sensory paradoxes (e.g., burning ice, ruby rain, coal-dark planets). Conversely, abstract psychological topics and brain tricks consistently underperform, indicating that the audience prefers grand, highly visual cosmic concepts over internal cognitive trivia.

winning_patterns.evidence: 'The Planet of Burning Ice Will Break Your Brain!' (1,055 views), 'The Planet Darker Than Coal: TrES-2b' (1,016 views), and 'This Planet Rains Supersonic Rubies!' (721 views) represent the top-tier performance.
winning_patterns.action: Double down on extreme cosmic conditions, focusing on highly visual, paradoxical, or high-value materials (e.g., gold, iron, acid, glass) in space.

weak_patterns.evidence: 'Your Brain Can Create Fake Memories' (multiple uploads peaking at only 53 views) and 'The Real Reason Songs Get Stuck In Your Head' (17 views) fail to capture audience interest.
weak_patterns.action: Phase out dry cognitive science and self-help brain hacks, or completely reframe them with cinematic, high-stakes storytelling.

next_video.concept: WASP-12b, a pitch-black egg-shaped planet being actively devoured and stretched by its parent star.
next_video.opening_direction: Right now, there is a planet in our galaxy being stretched and eaten alive.
next_video.twist_direction: But the terrifying part isn't just that it's being consumed—it's so pitch black that it absorbs almost all light, meaning its final moments are happening in absolute, silent darkness.
next_video.reason: Capitalizes on the proven success of extreme exoplanet facts (like TrES-2b and Burning Ice) by combining cosmic horror with a highly visual, tragic planetary fate.

experiment: Test a 'Cinematic Space Survival' micro-story format (e.g., 'What if you fell into a planet that rains molten iron?') to combine the high-performing exoplanet niche with immersive, first-person narrative storytelling.
